source.title: The Journey Matters: Average Parameter Count over Pre-training Unifies Sparse and Dense Scaling Laws
source.authors: Tian Jin; Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun; Utku Evci; Suvinay Subramanian; Amir Yazdanbakhsh; Dan Alistarh; G. Dziugaite

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether scaling-law relationships extend to sparse pre-training, a new training regime, and reports results for it.
record.gate_note: The study fits and evaluates a scaling law using average active parameter count for sparse and dense pre-training. Its pruning-schedule sweeps allocate compute among dense training, pruning, and recovery phases; they do not test how the loss-minimising parameter count and token count scale with a fixed compute budget. The downstream benchmark results compare a matched sparse–dense pair, but do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pre-training loss. Results cited from earlier scaling-law papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study fits the Chinchilla functional form, using average active parameter count, to 30 sparse and dense LLaMA-2 runs on C4. This tests whether the power-law loss form carries over to sparse pre-training, a new training regime (V5), and the dense runs also bear on V1. It does not test extrapolation (V2), compute-optimal allocation (V3), shape (V4) or downstream predictability (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that replacing N with average active parameter count lets the Chinchilla form model both sparse and dense loss, and that sparse pre-training matches dense quality at equal compute while yielding a smaller final model. They also prescribe pruning from 25% to 75% of training compute. Their Appendix B argues, by applying the law rather than testing it, that sparse training needs less data and lifetime compute.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates sparse pre-training and modifies the parameter-count input to the Chinchilla loss law to use average active parameters; it does not reproduce the original dense-model scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported fit error varies by sparsity level (0.007 at 0% and 0.03 at 60%); the compute–loss exponent for sparse 410M models differs across the two ranges divided at about 1e19 FLOPs.

fits_no_version.finding: A 1.14B-starting 50% sparse model and a dense model matched on average parameter count have near-identical downstream accuracy (geometric mean 42.42% vs 42.45%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse and dense models matched on average parameter count have similar downstream performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Near-optimal sparse pre-training allocates 25% of compute to dense training and 50% to pruning; the dense-optimal learning rate and batch size stay near-optimal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal sparse pre-training schedules transfer across sparsity levels and training durations.

record.problems: The scaling-law prediction error is reported on the same 30 data points used for fitting, rather than a held-out prediction set. The authors report a sparse compute–loss transition with different fitted slopes. They also state that their unstructured-sparsity implementation masks pruned parameters rather than eliminating their computation, and that actual compute may be up to 1/(1 − sparsity) times the estimated effective compute, reaching 5x at 80% sparsity.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. The sparsity-schedule and learning-rate/batch-size sweeps are not rows because they do not test parameter/token compute-optimal scaling.

untested.parts: Scaling over several orders of magnitude (only about 1 order in N); separate N, D and compute laws; held-out evaluation; the fitted coefficients are not reported.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer; sparse methods other than iterative magnitude pruning.
Comparison of fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions (beyond active vs final count), data choices, or compute-optimal splits across studies.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix B uses the fitted law to make allocation recommendations at 70B scale (uses_without_test for V3/V2); no extrapolation is checked against real runs. Effective compute for sparse models is scaled by sparsity, whereas the actual masked compute can be up to 5x higher. Peer reviewed at ICLR 2025.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not independently estimate loss scaling with parameters, tokens, and compute in bottleneck-free dense runs across several orders of magnitude. Its empirical fit uses average active parameter count and training tokens, and its compute-curve analysis is for sparse 410M models.

The study does not fit on small runs and then predict the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger. The reported fit error is on the 30 points used to fit the law; the larger-model appendix compares a matched sparse–dense pair.
The study does not measure how loss-minimising parameter count and token count scale with total compute.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at a fixed parameter count.
The study examines sparse and dense text pre-training, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Downstream benchmarks are reported for one matched sparse–dense pair, but the study does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pre-training loss.

The study reports a change in the compute–loss slope for sparse 410M models, but does not systematically compare parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, data choices, or compute-optimal allocation exponents across studies.

relationships.display_finding: The Chinchilla form achieved dense-run mean absolute error of 0.007 and overall fit error of 0.016 across 30 points.

relationships.reason: Fit error rises to 0.03 at 60% sparsity versus 0.007 for dense runs; the authors attribute this to unmodeled regularization effects of sparsity (R2).

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 5.3 reports the stated errors and attributes their disparity to unmodeled regularization, but still finds the common functional form sufficiently accurate. Larger residual error alone does not establish a condition where the power-law form fails or requires qualification.

relationships.condition: Within-run loss vs effective compute for sparse 410M models
relationships.reason: A single log-linear fit does not hold: the fitted slope changes from about 0.041 to 0.203 around 1e19 FLOPs. This is weak evidence because it is within-run, not a frontier (R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: Within sparse 410M training runs, the fitted slope changed from about 0.041 to 0.203 around 1e19 FLOPs, establishing a trajectory bend rather than a compute-frontier result.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Within-run loss vs effective compute for sparse 410M models
source_check.reason: Section 5.2 explicitly reports two fitted slopes, approximately 0.041 and 0.203, separated near 1e19 FLOPs. R6–R7 support bending of within-run trajectories, without establishing bending of a compute-optimal frontier.
